messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malik Okafor was thirty when the relationship ended, but the fractures it left behind outlasted the time. He remembered the second-floor apartment on Maple Drive, the way his former partner’s temper curdled into violence when the liquor bottles hit the floor. One evening, the air grew thick with the sharp, acrid scent of singed curtains after a shattered glass igniter caught fire. Malik had been shoved against the kitchen wall, his ribs cracking, as the flames licked the cabinets and his partner’s drunken shouts bounced off the peeling wallpaper. He had escaped through the back door, but the image of his own hands trembling, the burning fabric, and the suffocating fear never left him. When the relationship dissolved, his family had offered well-meaning but dismissive advice about staying together for the sake of tradition, remarks that mirrored the very minimization he had endured. That relational fracture, the alcohol, and the fire became the specific architecture of his trauma, ensuring that casual remarks about family, the scent of beer, and any hint of smoke would cut through his defenses long after the doors were locked. In the weeks that followed, Malik tried to rebuild his life as a curriculum designer for a private school, crafting lesson plans for teenagers who would never understand why he flinched when the office HVAC cycled on. Working in a glass-walled design studio, he learned to sit near the window and wear a thin layer of sandalwood cologne to mask the shared air system, which often carried the distant, metallic tang of burnt printer toner from the copy room. When a junior colleague mentioned his sister’s upcoming wedding and the pressure of family expectations, the casual reference acted as an immediate catalyst, dragging the full weight of the past event back into his mind. The recollection did not stay in his head; when it returned, he felt physical pain in the same parts of his body as during the event, a sharp, familiar ache across his ribs and shoulders that stole his breath before he could reach for his notebook. The scent of cheap whiskey on a passing student’s breath did not just startle him; it directly seeded a conviction that what happened to him was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it, hardening into a quiet, simmering resentment that made him decline every faculty mixer. The terror on recall did not fade with time; instead, it cemented his belief that he felt dirty or contaminated because of what happened, as if the violence had seeped into his skin and could never be washed away. He stopped showering for longer periods, scrubbing until his hands raw, convinced that maintaining physical cleanliness was the only way to preserve a shred of dignity in a world that had left him vulnerable. The more he scrubbed, the more isolated he became, and the more the memory of his own helplessness took root. He began to see the person he had become as unrecognisable to him, a man who jumped at closed doors and measured every conversation for hidden knives, abandoning the creative, collaborative work he once loved. Yet, as he isolated himself, the memory grew sharper, not weaker. Every time he forced himself to remember the event to anticipate future danger, the terror returned with greater force, which in turn made him hyper-vigilant to the smallest traces of alcohol or a burnt smell in his own apartment, in elevators, in passing cars. The smells would instantly flood his mind with the memory of the fire and the blows, and that sudden recollection would immediately flood him with the conviction that he was fundamentally tainted, that no apology or justice would ever restore the life he had lost. The cycle tightened with every shift he worked, every lesson plan he drafted with mechanical precision to keep his hands busy, every family-themed documentary he walked out of before the opening credits. Now, Malik sat in a therapist’s office for the first time, his palms sweating against his knees. He had finally sought help because the curriculum he spent his days designing felt hollow, a scaffolding built over a collapse he could no longer outrun. He was most afraid that the therapist would see him as broken beyond repair, but what he hoped for, quietly and without naming it, was to find a way to stop smelling smoke when the air was perfectly clean, and to meet someone without first bracing for the impact.
